name: Hùng Kings' Temple
summary: Temples on Nghĩa Lĩnh mountain dedicated to the Hùng Kings, the legendary founders of the first Vietnamese kingdom. Every spring, millions come to honour them.

hero.alt: The tomb of the Hùng King on Nghĩa Lĩnh mountain

eras.label: c. 500 BCE
eras.title: The kingdom of Văn Lang
eras.text: In the first millennium BCE, people of the Đông Sơn culture farmed rice and cast great bronze drums in the plains below this hill. Vietnamese tradition says that eighteen Hùng Kings ruled the kingdom of Văn Lang from nearby.

image.alt: The Well Temple at the foot of the mountain

eras.label: 15th century
eras.title: Writing down the legends
eras.text: Under the Lê dynasty, scholars compiled the stories of the Hùng Kings into an official genealogy. Temples on the mountain were rebuilt over the following centuries.

eras.title: A national day of remembrance
eras.text: The royal court fixed the 10th day of the third lunar month as the day to honour the Hùng Kings across the country. Today it is a public holiday.

eras.title: "Together we must defend it"
eras.text: In September 1954, Ho Chi Minh met soldiers at the temple and told them that the Hùng Kings had built the country, and that they must work together to defend it. The words are carved at the site.

image.alt: The gate of the temple complex

eras.title: A UNESCO tradition
eras.text: UNESCO added the worship of the Hùng Kings in Phú Thọ to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

eras.label: Today
eras.title: The spring pilgrimage
eras.text: During the festival season, crowds climb the stone steps through the forest, carrying incense, fruit and sticky-rice cakes to the temples at the top.

image.file: Trung tâm lễ hội đền Hùng 18-09-2015 1.jpg
image.alt: The festival centre at the foot of the mountain

story.title: Children of the Dragon and the Fairy
story.narration: Long ago, the legend says, Lạc Long Quân, a dragon lord of the sea, married Âu Cơ, a fairy of the mountains. She gave birth to a sac of one hundred eggs, which hatched into one hundred sons. But a dragon and a fairy could not live together for long. Fifty sons followed their father down to the sea, and fifty went with their mother into the mountains. The eldest of these became the first Hùng King. That is why Vietnamese people call each other đồng bào, 'born from the same sac'.

story.title: The prince and the rice cakes
story.narration: One Hùng King wanted to choose an heir, and asked his sons to bring him the finest dish for the new year. The princes searched land and sea for rare delicacies. The youngest, Lang Liêu, was poor. In a dream he was told to make cakes from the rice that feeds the people: a square one, bánh chưng, for the earth, and a round one, bánh giầy, for the sky. The king tasted them, understood their meaning, and made Lang Liêu his heir. Families still make bánh chưng every Lunar New Year.

story.title: Xoan, the songs of spring

image.file: Trung tâm lễ hội đền Hùng 18-09-2015 1.jpg

story.narration: In a few villages near Việt Trì, people have sung xoan for centuries at the start of each new year. It was performed in communal houses to honour the Hùng Kings and the village spirits, with drums and clappers, slow ritual songs and lively dances. By the early 2000s only a handful of elderly singers remained. UNESCO listed xoan as heritage in urgent need of safeguarding in 2011. Young people took up the songs, and in 2017 it was moved to the main list as a tradition that had been saved.

guide.price: Free entry. Small fees for parking and electric shuttles.

hours.notes: Approximate. Extremely crowded around the festival on the 10th day of the third lunar month.

do: Cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your hat inside the halls.
Walk around the main altar quietly, and let worshippers go first.
Wear comfortable shoes for the steps up the mountain.
Visit early in the morning to avoid crowds and heat.
dont: Point your feet at the altars or sit on temple steps in front of them.
Photograph people who are praying without asking.
Push in the queues during the festival.

tips.title: Local food
tips.text: Try bánh tai (rice dumplings), bánh chưng from the temple stalls, and Phú Thọ's sour pork (thịt chua).

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 1.5 hours from Hà Nội by car or bus; Việt Trì is 10 km away.

tips.title: The route
tips.text: From the gate, the path climbs past the Lower, Middle and Upper Temples to the tomb, then down to the Well Temple.
